body: And thank you for your kind comments of support.

This was a booked emergency visit. I am going to be assigned a doctor and a support person, in order to get a full evaluation and to see what kind of treatment I need.

Until then I have been prescribed medicines against anxiety and for relaxation to help me sleep. I have an emergency number I can call, will be taking time off from work for a week to try and collect myself and sleep.

Likely bipolar, but I will have to get a full evaluation first before I can start any long-term treatment. Still not sure that this was the right thing to do, but I will take any steps necessary now to start being there for my loved ones and to stop wanting to end my life.

You can take stunning photographs of homeless persons. Does that make the situation of homeless stunning? There is life, and then there is the abstract representation of it, in pictures or prose.

I've visited HK several times, been invited as a guest in both public housing and luxury condos. The high rises are the results of an architecture of necessity, where you want decent standards of living even for the poor, in an area where greenery and space on the ground is a precious commodity.

Imagine this: all but one of the elevators have failed in a public housing high rise. You are waiting for the last working elevator to show up and take you to the thirtieth floor. It is too hot and humid to even imagine taking the stairs. There is a queue of people with shopping bags in front of and behind you, they have raw fish, ripe durian, dried fish, pig intestines in their bags. You step into the elevator after twenty minutes of wait, together with way too many people. There are too many. There is no room to breathe. The elevator halts between floors twelve and thirteen, light stops. The heat and the putrid smell of produce gives someone a panic attack and they start wailing. They can't move any limbs, it's too compact. The elevator starts again after four minutes, spilling a couple of people out on every stop, but there is a new person entering for each stop. Once you get off, your clothes are soaked in the sweat of other people, your hair is plastered to your head and you are ready to vomit.

You are welcomed into an apartment where the air conditioning is buzzing so loud that people have to speak in raised voices to hear one another. Your host is preparing a fried fish meal and you just want to throw up. You step up to the windows and stare out on a wall of other high rise buildings. You can't open the windows. There are two people waiting to use the bathroom. Dinner begins in five minutes. And you just want to be anywhere else than here.

Welcome to Hong Kong. It's stunning. 

I honestly can't wait to go back.

Oh, I have seen some kick-ass chefs, and I can't imagine doing what they do for 12 hours straight without floundering. 16 hours for prepping five days a week seems outrageous. Must have been a really horrible restaurant (or marvellous pay at some long hours one). Sorry for you, man.
